issues.description: The negated condition complects two facts about a layer into one expression.
issues.detail: The new guard reads `!(nodeName === 'layer' && typeof node.nodes === 'undefined')`. The actual rule is: a layer with a block invalidates following imports; a bare layer statement does not. Naming that fact as a small predicate like `isLayerStatement(node)` would separate the *value* (what kind of layer is this) from the *control flow* (should we flag).

issues.description: `typeof node.nodes === 'undefined'` leans on a PostCSS implementation detail to decide semantics.
issues.detail: Whether a layer has a block is a fact about the parsed CSS, not about whether a property happens to be undefined on the AST node. PostCSS distinguishes AtRule from container nodes; checking `node.nodes` presence couples this rule to the current AST shape. A named helper keeps the implementation seam out of the rule body.

issues.description: The test covers the positive case but not the bare-layer negative case it implicitly redefines.
issues.detail: The fix changes the meaning of `@layer` from "always ignore" to "ignore only when blockless." A test asserting that `@layer foo, bar; @import ...` still passes would pin the new value semantics explicitly, so a future refactor cannot quietly re-complect the two layer forms.

review.summary: The fix is small and correct: a layer with a block is a different fact than a bare `@layer` statement, and the rule now distinguishes them. The concern is not behavior but decomposition — the predicate is inlined as a negated compound expression that reaches into a PostCSS AST detail (`typeof node.nodes === 'undefined'`). Pulling a named `isLayerStatement` (or `hasBlock`) helper would make the *value* — what kind of at-rule this is — explicit, separating it from the surrounding control flow. A companion test for the blockless `@layer` case would pin the new semantics. SIMPLE-ENOUGH, with one EASY-NOT-SIMPLE inline predicate worth naming.
